segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “To the angel of the assembly in Ephesus write: Thus says the one who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your works, your toil and your endurance, and that you cannot bear evil people. You have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and you have found them false.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You have endurance and have borne up for the sake of my name, and you have not grown weary.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I have this against you: you have abandoned the love you had at first.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Remember, then, from where you have fallen; turn back and do the works you did at first. If not, I am coming to you and will remove your lampstand from its place—unless you turn back.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But this you do have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And to the angel of the assembly in Smyrna write: Thus says the first and the last, who was dead and came to life:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your affliction and your poverty—yet you are rich—and the slander from those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Look, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison so that you may be tested, and you will have affliction for ten days. Be faithful to the point of death, and I will give you the crown of life.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies. The one who conquers will certainly not be harmed by the second death.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And to the angel of the assembly in Pergamum write: Thus says the one who has the sharp two-edged sword:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know where you live—where Satan’s throne is. Yet you hold fast to my name, and you did not deny your faith in me even in the days of Antipas, my witness, my faithful one, who was killed among you, where Satan lives.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold fast to the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat food sacrificed to idols and to commit sexual immorality.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In the same way, you too have some who hold fast to the teaching of the Nicolaitans.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Turn back, then. If not, I am coming to you soon and will make war on them with the sword of my mouth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will also give a white stone, and written on the stone a new name that no one knows except the one who receives it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And to the angel of the assembly in Thyatira write: Thus says the Son of God, whose eyes are like a flame of fire and whose feet are like burnished bronze:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your works, your love and faith and service and endurance, and that your latest works are greater than the first.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I have this against you: you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and who teaches and misleads my slaves into committing sexual immorality and eating food sacrificed to idols.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I gave her time to turn back, but she is not willing to turn back from her sexual immorality.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look, I am throwing her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her into great affliction, unless they turn back from her works;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and I will strike her children dead. Then all the assemblies will know that I am the one who searches minds and hearts, and I will give to each of you according to your works.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But to the rest of you in Thyatira, all who do not hold this teaching, who have not come to know the deep things of Satan, as they call them—to you I say: I am laying no other burden on you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Only hold fast to what you have until I come.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: To the one who conquers and keeps my works until the end I will give authority over the nations,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: to shepherd them with an iron rod, as clay pots are shattered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: just as I myself have received authority from my Father. And to that one I will give the morning star.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies.

notes.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution, so this translation uses “assembly” throughout. Most translations keep “church,” which readers readily understand; “assembly” can sound like a single meeting, but here it means the community of believers in a city.

The word means both “angel” and “messenger.” Most interpreters take the “angel” of each assembly as a heavenly being who represents the community, in line with the angels elsewhere in the book; others take it as a human messenger or leader. The messages address the angel in the singular but plainly speak to the whole community. The speaker throughout the chapter is the risen Jesus of the vision in chapter one.

notes.traditional: These things says; The words of
notes.note: The formula was already old-fashioned in first-century Greek. Readers knew it from the Septuagint, where it introduces the prophets’ “Thus says the Lord,” and it is also found in the proclamations of kings. Each of the seven messages opens with it, which gives them the tone of a prophetic oracle or a royal edict.

“Repent” now centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, which suits the command here to go back to the works done at first. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

The verb is the ordinary word for winning a battle, a contest or a court case, and is related to the noun for “victory.” “Overcome,” used by many translations, now tends to suggest merely getting past a difficulty. The meaning is not in dispute, and several modern versions also use “conquer” in Revelation.

The Greek is an ordinary word for hardship or oppression that bears down on someone, not a technical term. “Tribulation” is now heard by many readers as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the word does. The same word appears in verse 10 and in “great affliction” in verse 22.

John, himself Jewish, is describing a local conflict in Smyrna (and again in Philadelphia, 3:9), probably with members of the Jewish community who had spoken against the believers to their harm. The charge treats “Jews” as a name of honor that these opponents have forfeited, not as a term of reproach. Exactly who the group was is debated. The later use of the phrase against Jewish people in general is foreign to its setting.

Pergamum was a leading center of emperor worship in the Roman province of Asia and home to famous sanctuaries, including a great altar of Zeus and a shrine of the healing god Asclepius. Which of these the phrase points to is uncertain; many interpreters think of the imperial cult, since refusing to take part in it could be dangerous. Nothing is known of Antipas beyond this verse.

The verb covers unlawful sexual relations generally, but in the Greek version of the prophets it is also a standard image for unfaithfulness to God through idolatry. The story alluded to (Numbers 25 and 31:16) joins the two: Israelite men slept with Moabite women and joined in their sacrifices. Whether the teachers at Pergamum and Thyatira promoted actual sexual license, or the word is a figure for taking part in idol feasts, is disputed; the translation keeps the literal sense.

The word means a pebble of the kind used for voting and counting. Suggestions for the image include the white pebble a juror cast to acquit, a token giving admission to a feast, and an amulet inscribed with a secret name. None can be shown to be the one intended, and the meaning remains uncertain.

The Greek word is known only from Revelation (here and at 1:15), and its exact meaning is unknown. It clearly names some gleaming metal or alloy of copper; “burnished bronze” is the usual approximation.

This is almost certainly a symbolic name, not the woman’s own. Jezebel was the wife of Israel’s King Ahab, who promoted the worship of Baal and persecuted the Lord’s prophets (1 Kings 16–21). The name casts a prophet active in the Thyatira assembly as a new Jezebel leading God’s people into idolatry.

The Greek word is the ordinary one for a slave, a person who belongs to a master, not a hired servant. Most translations have “servants,” which softens this, though it reflects the fact that in the Septuagint the Lord’s “slaves” is also a title of honor for the prophets and for Israel. “Slaves” keeps the sense of belonging wholly to Christ.

The same Greek word is translated “Gentiles” elsewhere when it means the non-Jewish peoples. Verses 26–27 echo Psalm 2:8–9, where the peoples of the whole world are in view, so “nations” is used here.

The verb means to tend a flock and was a common image for a king’s government; the “rod” is both a shepherd’s club and a scepter. The line echoes the Greek version of Psalm 2:9, which has “shepherd” where the Hebrew text as traditionally read has “break.” Most translations have “rule,” and some scholars think the verb here means simply to rule or even to devastate. “Shepherd” keeps the image a Greek reader met, and the same verb is used of the Lamb at 7:17.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament and translators split between “slave” and “servant”; readers would be misled if Christ’s people are “slaves” in one chapter and “servants” in the next.

The πορνεία word group recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation (including the prostitute imagery of chapters 17–18), and renderings vary between “fornication,” “sexual immorality” and “prostitution.”
Used of Christ and of church leaders across several books, and in Revelation 2:27, 7:17, 12:5 and 19:15 translators split between “rule” and “shepherd,” hiding that it is one verb.
A key term in Paul, Hebrews, James and Revelation that is variously rendered “patience,” “perseverance,” “steadfastness” and “endurance.”
The word covers both abusive speech against people and against God, and a consistent rule is needed for when to use “slander” and when “blasphemy.”
